writing.exampleCaption: The unsafe block is small; the wrapper is where the rules live.
writing.explanation:
extern "C" fixes the calling convention, repr(C) fixes the layout, and everything about ownership becomes a convention you have to document. Who frees this pointer, may it be null, how long is it valid, and is it aliased are the four questions each call has to answer — and the safe wrapper you write around it is where those answers are enforced.

An FFI call joins two type systems at an ABI boundary. `extern "C"` selects the C calling convention, and `#[repr(C)]` requests a compatible struct layout for the target, including padding. The declarations on both sides must agree on integer widths, pointer types, alignment, and ownership. The Rust compiler cannot inspect a C header during an ordinary extern call to prove the declaration matches. A successful trivial call does not validate every edge case.

Take a function accepting a pointer and length. Ask whether the pointer may be null when length is zero, whether the callee reads or writes, whether it retains the pointer, and who frees the allocation. If Rust owns the buffer, it must remain alive throughout the foreign use. If C allocates a result, free it with the matching allocator specified by that API, not automatically with Rust's allocator. Wrap the unsafe call in a narrow function that checks lengths and translates error codes into `Result`.

For an interview, draw one value crossing the boundary and back. Include callback lifetime and thread assumptions if the C library calls into Rust later. Avoid exposing raw pointers to the rest of an application unless necessary. Test against the actual compiled library on each supported target, with boundary values and failures. The important point is the contract you can enforce on the Rust side and the assumptions you must trust on the foreign side.

Versioning is part of the boundary. A C library update can change a struct or function signature while Rust declarations remain stale. Compare headers and generated bindings against the linked library version in release checks. Keep opaque C types opaque on the Rust side when layout is not meant to be public.
